EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across La Crosse County from the evening of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 52 below zero at a mesonet station near St. Joseph. La Crosse city libraries closed due to the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following in behind a high wind/blizzard event, bitter cold arctic air along with northwest winds brought extreme wind chills to north central and northeast South Dakota.  The extreme wind chills began during the morning hours of the 29th and continued through the morning hours of the 31st.  Many record lows and record low maximums were set mainly on the 30th. Highs were in the teens below zero on the 30th across the east. Some of the record low temperatures were, 31 degrees below zero at Sisseton and Webster; 33 degrees below zero at Watertown; 37 degrees below zero at Eureka and Aberdeen; 38 degrees below zero at Summit; and 40 degrees below zero at Britton.||Most schools along with college campuses and businesses across the region had late starts or cancelled classes for two days. Mail service was also cancelled. Extreme wind chills from 35 degrees below to near 60 degrees below zero occurred. Some of the lowest wind chills include, 42 degrees below zero east of Danforth; 45 degrees below zero at Wallace; 47 degrees below zero at Aberdeen; 54 degrees below zero at Watertown; and 59 degrees below zero at Sisseton.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusty west winds ushered in a bitterly cold arctic air mass on January 30th into the morning hours of January 31st. Many businesses and schools were closed on both January 30th and January 31st due to this record breaking shot of dangerous cold air.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme cold arctic air surged into the northeast region January 30th. 500mb heights were close to 5040 meters, 850mb temperatures ranged from -26 to -30 degrees Celsius, and 925mb temperatures were near -22 to -26 degrees Celsius. With the quick drop in temperature in the boundary layer, a steep low level lapse rate was created near the surface. Due to this steep lapse rate, winds near 850mb to 925mb (averaging 20kts) were capable of reaching the surface and created wind chill temperatures of -22F and lower.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind chill of -25.0 F was measured near Accident, MD on Jan 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heading into the last few days of January, a historically cold air mass settled over the region. This led to a prolonged period a sub-zero temperatures and dangerously cold wind chills. Many schools were closed for 2-3 days due to the cold. The coldest temperatures were seen January 30th into the 31st. All 5 of our climate sites recorded record low high temperatures on the 30th and International Falls set a new record low the morning of the 31st. A run was also made at the Minnesota state record low temperature the morning of the 31st when a COOP site at Cotton, Minnesota, reached -56F, which is good for 5th coldest all-time. Wind chills during this stretch remained in the 30s and 40s below zero with numerous locations reaching into the 50s below zero during the early morning hours. Temperatures finally started warming on the 31st as the core of the high moved to the east and warmer air began to move in ahead of an area of low pressure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dangerous arctic air mass overspread northwest Ohio January 30th into the morning hours of January 31st. Wind chills between 25 and 45 degrees below zero were common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusty west winds ushered in a bitterly cold arctic air mass on January 30th into the morning hours of January 31st. The coldest of the air and strongest winds occurred during the morning hours of January 30th when the wind chill value at Defiance  dropped to 36 degrees below zero. Wind chills through the event generally ranged between 25 and 45 degrees below zero. The coldest air temperature recorded at Defiance was 14 degrees below zero on January 30th. Many businesses and schools were closed on both January 30th and January 31st due to this record breaking shot of dangerous cold air.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heading into the last few days of January, a historically cold air mass settled over the region. This led to a prolonged period a sub-zero temperatures and dangerously cold wind chills. Many schools were closed for 2-3 days due to the cold. The coldest temperatures were seen January 30th into the 31st. All 5 of our climate sites recorded record low high temperatures on the 30th and International Falls set a new record low the morning of the 31st. A run was also made at the Minnesota state record low temperature the morning of the 31st when a COOP site at Cotton, Minnesota, reached -56F, which is good for 5th coldest all-time. Wind chills during this stretch remained in the 30s and 40s below zero with numerous locations reaching into the 50s below zero during the early morning hours. Temperatures finally started warming on the 31st as the core of the high moved to the east and warmer air began to move in ahead of an area of low pressure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme cold arctic air surged into the northeast region January 30th. 500mb heights were close to 5040 meters, 850mb temperatures ranged from -26 to -30 degrees Celsius, and 925mb temperatures were near -22 to -26 degrees Celsius. With the quick drop in temperature in the boundary layer, a steep low level lapse rate was created near the surface. Due to this steep lapse rate, winds near 850mb to 925mb (averaging 20kts) were capable of reaching the surface and created wind chill temperatures of -22F and lower.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind chill of -30.0 F was measured at Monaca, PA on Jan 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong arctic high pressure system brought historic cold to much of the Midwest January 29th through January 31st.  Numerous low temperature records were broken, including all-time record lows at Moline.  A state record low temperature was observed by the Mount Carroll Cooperative Observer on January 31st when they record a low of -38F. In addition, life threatening wind chills were reported with values below -30 degrees for many hours.  Numerous schools, churches, and businesses closed during the arctic outbreak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The lowest wind chill at the Freeport AWOS was -53 at 555 AM on January 30th.

A state record low temperature was observed by the Mount Carroll Cooperative Observer on January 31st when they record a low of -38F. In addition, life threatening wind chills were reported with values below -30 degrees for many hours.  Numerous schools, churches, and businesses closed during the arctic outbreak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The lowest wind chill at the Dubuque ASOS was -55 at at 653 AM on January 30th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heading into the last few days of January, an historically cold air mass settled over the region. This led to a prolonged period a sub-zero temperatures and dangerously cold wind chills. Many schools were closed for 2-3 days due to the cold. The coldest temperatures were seen January 30th into the 31st. All 5 of our climate sites recorded record low high temperatures on the 30th. Wind chills during this stretch remained in the 20s and 30s below zero with numerous locations reaching into the 40s below zero during the early morning hours. Temperatures finally started warming on the 31st as the core of the high moved to the east and warmer air began to move in ahead of an area of low pressure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Adams County from the evening of January 29th into the morning of the 31st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One person died from hypothermia in Rochester (Olmsted County) on January 30th after being stranded outside a house overnight. The coldest wind chill to occur was 63 below zero near Dexter (Mower County) and near Ridgeway (Winona County) during the early morning of January 30th. Most southeast Minnesota schools were closed January 29th through the 31st. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of southeast Minnesota on January 30th and 31st. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusty west winds ushered in a bitterly cold arctic air mass late on January 29th through the morning hours of January 31st. The coldest of the air and strongest winds occurred during the morning hours of January 30th when the wind chill value near La Porte dropped to 46 degrees below zero. Wind chills through the event generally ranged between 25 and 50 degrees below zero. The coldest air temperature recorded at La Porte was 25 degrees below zero on January 31st. Many businesses and schools were closed on both January 30th and January 31st due to this record breaking shot of dangerous cold air. Gusty winds up to 40 mph also led to areas of blowing and drifting snow that helped wreak havoc on area roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heading into the last few days of January, an historically cold air mass settled over the region. This led to a prolonged period a sub-zero temperatures and dangerously cold wind chills. Many schools were closed for 2-3 days due to the cold. The coldest temperatures were seen January 30th into the 31st. All 5 of our climate sites recorded record low high temperatures on the 30th. Wind chills during this stretch remained in the 20s and 30s below zero with numerous locations reaching into the 40s below zero during the early morning hours. Temperatures finally started warming on the 31st as the core of the high moved to the east and warmer air began to move in ahead of an area of low pressure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Buffalo County from the afternoon of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 52 below zero at a mesonet station in Cochrane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme cold arctic air surged into the northeast region January 30th. 500mb heights were close to 5040 meters, 850mb temperatures ranged from -26 to -30 degrees Celsius, and 925mb temperatures were near -22 to -26 degrees Celsius. With the quick drop in temperature in the boundary layer, a steep low level lapse rate was created near the surface. Due to this steep lapse rate, winds near 850mb to 925mb (averaging 20kts) were capable of reaching the surface and created wind chill temperatures of -22F and lower.

Gusty winds up to 40 mph also led to areas of blowing and drifting snow that helped wreak havoc on area roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Clark County from the afternoon of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 53 below zero at a mesonet station in Loyal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme cold arctic air surged into the northeast region January 30th. 500mb heights were close to 5040 meters, 850mb temperatures ranged from -26 to -30 degrees Celsius, and 925mb temperatures were near -22 to -26 degrees Celsius. With the quick drop in temperature in the boundary layer, a steep low level lapse rate was created near the surface. Due to this steep lapse rate, winds near 850mb to 925mb (averaging 20kts) were capable of reaching the surface and created wind chill temperatures of -22F and lower.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Surrounding areas had wind chill values below -25 F.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gusty west winds ushered in a bitterly cold arctic air mass late on January 29th through the morning hours of January 31st. The coldest of the air and strongest winds occurred during the morning hours of January 30th when the wind chill value at Majenica dropped to 45 degrees below zero. Wind chills through the event generally ranged between 25 and 50 degrees below zero. The coldest air temperature recorded at Huntington was 22 degrees below zero on January 31st. Many businesses and schools were closed due to this record breaking shot of dangerous cold air.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Crawford County from the evening of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 52 degrees below zero at the automated weather observing equipment for the Prairie du Chien airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough carried cold air into the Northeast Region on January 21st. A 5200 meter height was recorded at 500mb, 850mb temperatures were -22C to -25C, and 925mb temperatures were -18C to -21C. The wind gust average throughout the area was 25mph while the ridges experienced higher gusts due to a tight pressure gradient from an exiting surface low pressure. The positioning of a building high pressure in the Midwest helped keep wind speeds west of the ridges fairly light.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind chill of -16.0 F was measured near Tunnelton, WV on the morning of Jan 21st. Surrounding areas got below -25 F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

Although temperatures slowly modified above the surface past the afternoon of Tuesday, January 29th, the combination of very strong winds and temperatures in the teens and 20s below zero, wind chill values averaged between 45 and 59 degrees below zero from Tuesday afternoon, through Wednesday morning. Although wind speeds lowered on Wednesday, actual temperatures in the 20s and 30s below zero kept wind chill values below -35F through Thursday morning. ||The coldest measured wind chill of -59F in west central Wisconsin was at the Menomonie airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several local weather sources measured wind chill values lower than -35F from Tuesday afternoon, through Thursday morning. The coldest wind chill was -57F at the Cumberland airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Grant County from the evening of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 55 below zero at the automated weather observing equipment for the Platteville airport. Near Hazel Green, one person was outside for about an hour and suffered hypothermia related injuries. A power outage during the morning of January 30th affected about 360 households in Boscobel and Blue River and the surrounding rural areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough carried cold air into the Northeast Region on January 21st. A 5200 meter height was recorded at 500mb, 850mb temperatures were -22C to -25C, and 925mb temperatures were -18C to -21C. The wind gust average throughout the area was 25mph while the ridges experienced higher gusts due to a tight pressure gradient from an exiting surface low pressure. The positioning of a building high pressure in the Midwest helped keep wind speeds west of the ridges fairly light.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind chill temperature of -29.0 degrees F was measured on January 21st at 8am (2 miles NNE of Accident,MD).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous wind chills occurred during the late evening hours on January 29th across portions of north central Nebraska. Temperatures near 10 below zero combined with north winds of 10 to 20 mph to produce wind chills of 30 to 35 below zero.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A nearby mesonet site located 10 miles southeast of Mills recorded a minimum wind chill of 30 degrees below zero at 1120 pm CST on December 29th. Another nearby mesonet site located 8 miles north northwest of Butte recorded a minimum wind chill of 34 degrees below zero at 945 pm CST on December 29th. Dangerous wind chills from 30 to 35 below occurred across Boyd County during the late evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The largest snowstorm to date in the 2018-19 winter occurred on January 19th and 20th across eastern New York. Low pressure formed over the lower Mississippi Valley and lifted northeast across the Tennessee Valley during the night of the 19th before moving along the Mason-Dixon line on the 20th. Strong rising motion occurred as southerly winds aloft transported moist air northward, which was lifted over the cold airmass in place over eastern New York. Snowfall broke out during the afternoon of the 19th, continuing heavy at times into the evening and overnight hours before ending during the morning of the 20th. The strong southerly flow brought above-freezing air aloft into the region, causing the snow to turn to sleet as far north as the Capital District and northern Catskills for a time before turning back to snow. Further south, the air aloft was warm enough to turn the precipitation to freezing rain with ice accretion of one to three tenths of an inch over portions of the southeast Catskills, Mid-Hudson Valley, and southern Taconics.||Snowfall totals were heaviest from the central Mohawk Valley into the southern Adirondacks and Lake George-Saratoga region where 1.5 to 2 foot totals were common. Three to six inches of snow and sleet along with some ice occurred over the Mid- Hudson Valley, while the remainder of the region saw between 6 and 18 inches.||The snowfall resulted in the cancellation of many weekend activities along with all flights from Albany International Airport scheduled to leave the morning and afternoon of the 20th. The governor of New York banned buses and tractor trailers from nearly the entire New York State Thruway and most interstate highways during the storm. States of emergency were declared for Albany and Saratoga Counties. Also, around 200 customers lost power due to the freezing rain in Ulster and Dutchess Counties. ||Frigid temperatures followed the snow for Monday and Tuesday, January 21st-22nd, with wind chills falling to -20 to -40F across most of the region. The cold weather prompted the closing of schools and the opening of warming shelters across the region.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero were common across Richland County from the evening of January 29th into the morning of the 31st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winter continued its grip on Iowa, with persistent cold air advection after the departure of a combination of blizzard conditions, freezing rain, and blowing snow. As the parent surface low and 500 mb trough departed the area, through the 7th of February, gusty northwest winds to 20 to 25+ mph ushered in a push of Arctic air that peaked overnight on the 7th into the morning of the 8th. As a result, morning lows dropped down to around -10 degrees F across portions of northern and northwest Iowa, while near zero to below zero temperatures prevailed all the way to the Iowa-Missouri border.  While the surface pressure gradient and resulting winds relaxed through the evening of the 7th, the bitter cold did not require strong winds to result in persistent -25 to -35 degree F wind chill values overnight and into the morning hours. Winds in the 10 to 20 mph range were sufficient to achieve the previously mentioned wind chill values.  Incoming surface high pressure continued to relax winds, allowing wind chill values to warm above the -20 degrees F range or warmer by noon on the 8th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure situated over the eastern Pacific and a slow moving upper level closed low over the Great Lakes combined to put the upper Midwest, including Iowa, right in the cross hairs of northwest upper level flow and an Arctic air mass intrusion. Air temperatures plummeted below zero the evening of the 29th across much of the state, and did not rise back above zero in most locations until the afternoon on the 31st. Coldest temperatures were seen across northern and northeast Iowa where temperatures in the 20 to nearly 30 below range were common.  Given the temperatures, even nominal winds put areas into Wind Chill Advisory (-20 to -30 degrees F) with ease. Throughout the time period, many locations experienced wind chill values in the -40 to -55 degrees F range which were some of the coldest wind chills in over two decades.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With arctic air in place over western Wisconsin, air temperatures dropped into the 20s below zero from January 29th into January 31st. A few sites recorded temperatures in the 30s below zero on the morning of the 30th with several sites falling into the 30s and 40s below zero on the morning of the 31st. When combined with wind speeds of 5 to 25 mph, wind chills of 35 to 60 below were common. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero in Medford (Taylor County) during the morning of January 30th. One person suffered hypothermia related injuries near Hazel Green (Grant County) when they were found outdoors after about an hour. A power outage occurred across northern Grant County during the morning of January 30th that affected approximately 360 households. The Governor of Wisconsin declared a state of emergency because of the cold weather. Most western Wisconsin schools were closed from January 28th through the 31st. La Crosse (La Crosse County) city libraries closed because of the cold and this had never occurred in the past 34 years. The U.S. Post Office suspended delivery operations across all of western Wisconsin on January 30th and 31st. Classes at UW-La Crosse were canceled on January 30th and 31st while both Viterbo and Western Technical College canceled classes on the 30th and the morning of the 31st. More than 1,000 elderly people across La Crosse County did not receive meals during the cold outbreak as the county's senior nutrition program was closed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills of 35 to 60 below zero were common across Taylor County from the late afternoon of January 29th into the morning of the 31st. The coldest wind chill to occur was 57 below zero at the automated weather observing equipment for the Medford airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surge of historically cold arctic air settled over southern WI. Windy conditions and low temperatures in the -20s to -30s Fahrenheit resulted in wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero for much of this period. High temperatures did not warm above 10 below zero for most locations on January 30th. Widespread government, school, and business closings were common on January 30-31st. The United States Postal Service suspended mail delivery on January 29-30th. Many water main breaks occurred especially in Madison and Milwaukee. Power outages occurred over portions of Milwaukee, Waukesha, Racine, and Kenosha Counties as power lines constricted and snapped in the extreme cold. A man was found frozen in his garage in Milwaukee and had collapsed after shoveling snow. Another man was found frozen in the snow in Cudahy and died from hypothermia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero.

Windy conditions and low temperatures in the -20s to -30s Fahrenheit resulted in wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero for much of this period. High temperatures did not warm above 10 below zero for most locations on January 30th. Widespread government, school, and business closings were common on January 30-31st. The United States Postal Service suspended mail delivery on January 29-30th. Many water main breaks occurred especially in Madison and Milwaukee. Power outages occurred over portions of Milwaukee, Waukesha, Racine, and Kenosha Counties as power lines constricted and snapped in the extreme cold. A man was found frozen in his garage in Milwaukee and had collapsed after shoveling snow. Another man was found frozen in the snow in Cudahy and died from hypothermia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region on the morning of January 29 and departed into Canada. In the wake of this low, an arctic cold front moved through the lower Great Lakes region early on January 29, allowing for arctic high pressure to build over the midwest, setting up an extremely cold pattern for January 29 - 31. The blistering cold that entered the region resulted in temperatures on January 30 and 31 being some of the coldest recorded in five years. A strong pressure gradient set up over the region between the departing low pressure system and the incoming surface high resulting in winds to 30 - 35 mph across the region. These strong winds along with the extreme cold allowed for wind chills to drop below zero degrees by midday on January 29 and not return above zero until late on January 31. The coldest temperatures during this event were on the morning of January 30 with several locations approaching or exceeding record low temperatures in the -5F to -11F range. During these coldest temperatures, the wind chill reached -25F for several hours across the entire area with several locations reaching wind chill values of -35F to -40F for a time. Temperatures on January 30 stayed near or below zero for much of the day and dropped back below zero on the morning of January 31. Record low temperatures were set again on January 31, but the winds had subsided to 15 to 20 mph across the area, allowing for wind chills in the -15F to -20F range. Temperatures reached the upper single digits during the day on January 31 and winds subsided to light and variable, ending the extreme cold threat. Four deaths were reported in Ohio as a result of the extreme cold. All area schools closed on both January 30 and 31 due to the cold conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extremely cold weather settled over the area on January 30 and 31, bringing the coldest temperatures that the region had seen in four or five years. With winds gusting to 30 - 35 mph, wind chills across the county dropped below zero midday on January 29 and did not recover to above zero until late on January 31. Wind chills reached -25F for a period on January 30 with wind chills of -30F to -35F being noted during the late morning hours. All area schools were closed on January 30 and 31 due to the extreme cold.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surge of historically cold arctic air settled over southern WI. Windy conditions and low temperatures in the -20s to -30s Fahrenheit resulted in wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero for much of this period. High temperatures did not warm above 10 below zero for most locations on January 30th. Widespread government, school, and business closings were common on January 30-31st. The United States Postal Service suspended mail delivery on January 29-30th. Many water main breaks occurred especially in Madison and Milwaukee. Power outages occurred over portions of Milwaukee, Waukesha, Racine, and Kenosha Counties as power lines constricted and snapped in the extreme cold. A man was found frozen in his garage in Milwaukee and had collapsed after shoveling snow. Another man was found frozen in the snow in Cudahy and died from hypothermia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero.

A frigid air mass had settled over the area as well, with morning lows on the 3rd generally from 15 below to 25 below zero. Combined with the steady winds, wind chills dipped to the 40s below zero. The coldest wind chill was Fosston and Dilworth, at 46 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system moved through the Great Lakes region on the morning of January 29 and departed into Canada. In the wake of this low, an arctic cold front moved through the lower Great Lakes region early on January 29, allowing for arctic high pressure to build over the midwest, setting up an extremely cold pattern for January 29 - 31. The blistering cold that entered the region resulted in temperatures on January 30 and 31 being some of the coldest recorded in five years. A strong pressure gradient set up over the region between the departing low pressure system and the incoming surface high resulting in winds to 30 - 35 mph across the region. These strong winds along with the extreme cold allowed for wind chills to drop below zero degrees by midday on January 29 and not return above zero until late on January 31. The coldest temperatures during this event were on the morning of January 30 with several locations approaching or exceeding record low temperatures in the -5F to -11F range. During these coldest temperatures, the wind chill reached -25F for several hours across the entire area with several locations reaching wind chill values of -35F to -40F for a time. Temperatures on January 30 stayed near or below zero for much of the day and dropped back below zero on the morning of January 31. Record low temperatures were set again on January 31, but the winds had subsided to 15 to 20 mph across the area, allowing for wind chills in the -15F to -20F range. Temperatures reached the upper single digits during the day on January 31 and winds subsided to light and variable, ending the extreme cold threat. Four deaths were reported in Ohio as a result of the extreme cold. All area schools closed on both January 30 and 31 due to the cold conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extremely cold weather settled over the area on January 30 and 31, bringing the coldest temperatures that the region had seen in four or five years. Low temperatures at Youngstown-Warren Regional Airport reached -5F on January 30 and -7F on January 31. With winds gusting to 30 - 35 mph, wind chills across the county dropped below zero midday on January 29 and did not recover to above zero until late on January 31. At Youngstown-Warren Regional Airport, wind chills reached -25F for a period on January 30 and the lowest wind chill recorded during the event was -30F during the late morning hours of the 30th. All area schools were closed on January 30 and 31 due to the extreme cold.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extremely cold arctic air dominated the weather across central and northeast South Dakota from the late evening of the 2nd through the morning of the 3rd. Record lows in the teens below and 20s below zero were set across the region. Most of the record lows shattered the previous record lows by 5 to 10 degrees. In fact, Britton in northeast South Dakota fell to 29 degrees below zero breaking the old record of 19 degrees below zero.||The arctic cold along with north winds brought dangerously cold wind chills ranging from 35 below zero to near 55 below zero across the region. Some of the extreme wind chills included, 40 degrees below zero at Aberdeen; 42 degrees below zero at Pierre; 45 degrees below zero at Holabird; 46 degrees below zero at Barnard; 47 degrees below zero at Gettysburg; 49 degrees below zero at Britton and Eureka; and 53 degrees below zero south of Bullhead.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NA

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surge of historically cold arctic air settled over southern WI. Windy conditions and low temperatures in the -20s to -30s Fahrenheit resulted in wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero for much of this period. High temperatures did not warm above 10 below zero for most locations on January 30th. Widespread government, school, and business closings were common on January 30-31st. The United States Postal Service suspended mail delivery on January 29-30th. Many water main breaks occurred especially in Madison and Milwaukee. Power outages occurred over portions of Milwaukee, Waukesha, Racine, and Kenosha Counties as power lines constricted and snapped in the extreme cold. A man was found frozen in his garage in Milwaukee and had collapsed after shoveling snow. Another man was found frozen in the snow in Cudahy and died from hypothermia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures of 35 below to 55 below zero.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Winter continued its grip on Iowa, with persistent cold air advection after the departure of a combination of blizzard conditions, freezing rain, and blowing snow. As the parent surface low and 500 mb trough departed the area, through the 7th of February, gusty northwest winds to 20 to 25+ mph ushered in a push of Arctic air that peaked overnight on the 7th into the morning of the 8th. As a result, morning lows dropped down to around -10 degrees F across portions of northern and northwest Iowa, while near zero to below zero temperatures prevailed all the way to the Iowa-Missouri border.  While the surface pressure gradient and resulting winds relaxed through the evening of the 7th, the bitter cold did not require strong winds to result in persistent -25 to -35 degree F wind chill values overnight and into the morning hours. Winds in the 10 to 20 mph range were sufficient to achieve the previously mentioned wind chill values.  Incoming surface high pressure continued to relax winds, allowing wind chill values to warm above the -20 degrees F range or warmer by noon on the 8th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between late evening of February 8th and late morning of the 9th, an Arctic cold front moved from near the I-90 corridor in western and southwest Montana to a position extending southeastward from northwestern Idaho to east-central Idaho. Behind this front, a strong Arctic high pressure ridge settled southward across north-central and southwest Montana. This ridge was accompanied by a tight surface pressure gradient, especially over southwest Montana and along the Rocky Mountain Front. The tight pressure gradient resulted in breezy surface winds. In turn, the combination of these winds and frigid temperatures yielded warning-criteria wind chills for parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Citizen Weather Observer Program (CWOP) station recorded wind chill of -41F accompanied by sustained wind of 25 mph. Location: 2-miles NNW of Joplin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning of Wednesday, February 12th, an Arctic front moved rapidly southward across the Dakotas, and into Minnesota. Temperatures fell 10 to 20 degrees in less than a couple hours as this front moved through the area. Along with the falling temperatures, wind speeds increased to 25 to 35 mph, with gusts in the 40 to 50 mph range in west central Minnesota by mid-morning, and across southwest/south central Minnesota by afternoon. Light snow accompanied the front, but as winds increased, visibility dropped to less than one quarter of a mile. This was noted on several weather sensors, including the Minnesota Department of Transportation. Local webcams, and MNDOT mobile cameras also supported the blizzard conditions. The worst conditions occurred along the South Dakota, Minnesota border where the strongest winds were reported. Satellite imagery also noted the contrast of where blowing snow occurred, and where skies were clear. ||By the mid to late afternoon, temperatures fell well below zero in west-central Minnesota, with wind chills already exceeding -35F in Stevens County. These cold wind chills expanded south and east across Minnesota, and by the evening a broad area of wind chill values of -35 to -45 degrees developed. These wind chill values lasted through Thursday morning before temperatures rose, and wind speeds decreased.||Some of the lowest wind chill values during this time include:|-48F at Benson.|-46 at St. James.|-45 at Fairmont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historic outbreak of arctic air resulted in record breaking cold temperatures during an extreme cold spell that lasted almost two weeks for some locations across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. The cold air moved over the northeastern combined Panhandles as early as Feb 8th, and spread southwest through Feb 12th, engulfing most of the southern plains by Feb 13th. The northeast Panhandles remained below freezing for 12 days straight while the southwest Panhandles were below freezing for a full week or more. Periods of flurries and freezing fog also occurred mainly in the overnight and morning periods almost each day Feb 8th through Feb 18th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very bitter arctic air with ambient temperatures dropping to near zero or below zero and north winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts to near 30 mph on February 14, continued into the morning of February 15.  These factors resulted in extreme wind chill warning criteria reaching -18 degrees or colder for several hours for the northern areas of West Central Texas. There was also damage to pipes, public utility systems and water supply systems across the region.  Many were left without water for days.  Dollar damages will be well into the millions across West Central Texas.  The specific and complete information relating to the fatalities and monetary damages will gradually become available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-February 2021 unleashed a relentless blast of brutal cold, the likes of which North Central Kansas had not endured in several decades. Of the few long-time NWS cooperative observer temperature stations within the six-county area, the 10-day stretch from the 7th-16th marked the overall-coldest 10 days in either 32 years (since Dec. 1989) or 38 years (since Dec. 1983)...based on average/mean temperature. Focusing specifically on the Smith Center observer data (84 years of available records), the 10-day average temperature between the 7th-16th was -0.3 degrees (F), an incredible 32 degrees below the 30-year normal. Daily highs over the course of the 10 days ranged from -2 to +14 degrees, while daily lows ranged from -20 to 0. Among other temperature tidbits for Smith Center, nine straight days of sub-zero lows at the official NWS observer station matched the previous record first achieved in Dec. 1983, and the nearby unofficial airport AWOS spent AROUND 45 HOURS AT-OR-BELOW ZERO between the early afternoon of the 14th and late morning of the 16th (this likely hadn't occurred since at least Feb. 1989). In addition, the low temperature of -20 on the 15th set a new February record (coldest low since Dec. 1989), while the high temperature of -2 on the 15th matched the existing February record first set in 1989. Factoring in winds (albeit relatively light through the majority of the 10-day period), the most frigid wind chill readings occurred between the evening of the 14th and the morning of the 16th, prompting a long-fuse Wind Chill Warning for all of North Central Kansas. On both mornings of the 15th and 16th, a handful of unofficial automated stations recorded wind chill values well down into the -30 to -40 range, highlighted by -37 at mesonet stations near Lebanon and Kirwin on the 15th and -37 at Smith Center airport on the 16th. ||Focusing on impacts, the local North Central Kansas area was just a tiny sliver of an expansive swath of the central and southern United States that battled this historic cold, as sub-freezing temperatures surged all the way into south Texas (even promoting a light coating of snow at Galveston). This cold outbreak put a considerable strain on not only the local, but especially the regional power and energy industry. While North Central Kansas avoided more serious/longer-lasting power disruptions that ravaged many southern states, fairly brief rolling blackouts (typically around 30 minutes) occurred within the area on the 15th-16th, as called for by the Southwest Power Pool (the independent regional transmission organization that manages the electric grid and wholesale power market for portions of 14 central and southern states, including Kansas). Turning to the large-scale meteorological picture, this prolonged/intense cold outbreak was driven in the mid-upper levels by a parade of troughs circulating around a quasi-stationary parent vortex churning over southern Canada, each one further reinforcing/intensifying the magnitude of Arctic air allowed to spill southward through the central United States. At the surface, persistent, predominantly northerly flow prevailed for days on end as a sprawling Arctic high increasingly-dominated much of the central and northeastern United States. Also contributing to the magnitude of persistent cold in North Central Kansas was a variable blanket of snow cover, generally ranging from 1-2 inches south of Highway 24 to as deep as 6-9 inches in some areas along/north of Highway 36, where a series of snow events brushed the area between the 6th-14th. Concluding with a brief rundown of how North Central Kansas finally crawled out from underneath the 10-day crush of ruthless cold, improvement finally got underway on the 17th and trended upward for several days thereafter, with high temperatures across most of the area recovering into the teens on the 17th, 20s on the 18th, 30s-40s on the 19th (ending a 13-day sub-freezing streak at Smith Center), 40s-50s on the 20th, and even reaching the 70s by the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The following are the coldest recorded wind chills for the period: on the morning of Feb. 15th: -37 degrees two miles south of Lebanon; -35 degrees at Smith Center Airport AWOS. On the morning of Feb. 16th: -37 degrees at Smith Center Airport AWOS; -33 degrees two miles south of Lebanon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very bitter arctic air with ambient temperatures dropping to near zero or below zero and north winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts to near 30 mph on February 14, continued into the morning of February 15.  These factors resulted in extreme wind chill warning criteria reaching -18 degrees or colder for several hours for the northern areas of West Central Texas.  There were a few reports of -20 to -24 degree wind chill readings.  Another period of extreme cold occurred late on February 15 and continued into morning of February 16 mainly across the higher elevation areas of the northern portions of West Central Texas where the winds were a little stronger.  Wind chill temperatures were estimated for some locations since the wind sensors at several weather stations froze because of ice.  There were also widespread power outages during this extreme cold as a result of a failing power grid.   Many residents were left with out power Monday through Tuesday and some even longer.  These very cold temperatures and widespread power outages resulted in several deaths caused by hypothermia.  There was also damage to pipes, public utility systems and water supply systems across the region.  Many were left without water for days.  Dollar damages will be well into the millions across West Central Texas.  The specific and complete information relating to the fatalities and monetary damages will gradually become available.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill temperatures from the Texas Tech West Texas Mesonet site located at Fort Chadbourne measured a wind chill temperature below -18.  The coldest wind chill was -19 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-February 2021 unleashed a relentless blast of brutal cold, the likes of which South Central Nebraska had not endured in several decades. For the majority of the 24-county area, the 10-day stretch from the 7th-16th marked the overall-coldest 10 days in nearly 38 years...since December 1983 (based on average/mean temperature). In addition to various other official NWS stations (including both automated airport sensors and cooperative observers), this fact rang true for Grand Island and Hastings airports, where the 10-day average temperature from the 7th-16th was -4.7 and -5.5 degrees (F), respectively. Following are various other cold temperature tidbits specifically for Grand Island (126 years of temperature records) and Hastings (114 years of records), although very similar realities applied elsewhere within South Central Nebraska. At Grand Island, the average temperature between the 7th-16th was an incredible 33 degrees below the 30-year normal, as daily highs over the course of the 10 days ranged from -7 to +10, while daily lows ranged from -27 to +1. Furthermore, Grand Island notched nine straight days of sub-zero lows between the 8th-16th (longest such streak since Dec. 1989), and both Grand Island and Hastings spent OVER 60-CONSECUTIVE HOURS BELOW ZERO between the early morning of the 14th and the afternoon/evening of the 16th (had not happened since at least Feb. 1989). At Hastings, the high temperature of -8 on the 15th set a new February record for coldest daily high and was only one-degree short of the record-coldest high (for any month) of -9 set in Dec. 1989. Perhaps most impressively, Hastings plunged to -30 for the low on the 16th, tying its all-time coldest reading first observed way back in Jan. 1912. A few long-time NWS coop observer stations actually set outright all-time coldest low temperatures on the 16th, including York (-34), Superior (-33) and Osceola (-31). Greeley and Ord airport (ASOS) matched the York reading of -34 for the outright-coldest official temperature of this particular cold snap. Factoring in winds (albeit relatively light through the majority of the 10-day period), the most frigid wind chill readings occurred between the evening of the 14th and the morning of the 16th, prompting a long-fuse Wind Chill Warning for all of South Central Nebraska. On both mornings of the 15th and 16th, dozens of automated stations (official and unofficial) recorded wind chill values well down into the -30 to -45 range, and even a few that breached -50. While each morning registered fairly similar and dangerously-cold values area-wide, the morning of the 15th featured both the coldest known official wind chill (-54 at Ord airport ASOS) and unofficial wind chill (-55 from a NDOT sensor two miles south of Elm Creek). ||Focusing on impacts, the local South Central Nebraska area was just a small portion of an expansive swath of the central and southern United States that battled this historic cold, as sub-freezing temperatures surged all the way into south Texas (even promoting a light coating of snow at Galveston). This cold outbreak put a considerable strain on not only the local, but especially the regional power and energy industry. While South Central Nebraska avoided more serious/longer-lasting power disruptions that ravaged many southern states, fairly brief rolling blackouts (typically around 30 minutes) occurred within the area on the 15th-16th, as called for by the Southwest Power Pool (the independent regional transmission organization that manages the electric grid and wholesale power market for portions of 14 central and southern states, including Nebraska). Turning to the large-scale meteorological picture, this prolonged/intense cold outbreak was driven in the mid-upper levels by a parade of troughs circulating around a quasi-stationary parent vortex churning over southern Canada, each one further reinforcing/intensifying the magnitude of Arctic air allowed to spill southward through the central United States. At the surface, persistent, predominantly northerly flow prevailed for days on end as a sprawling Arctic high increasingly-dominated much of the central and northeastern United States. Also contributing to the magnitude of persistent cold in South Central Nebraska was increasingly-deep snow cover, as a series of snow events gradually boosted the average snow depth across the area from generally 2-5 inches on the 5th (just prior to the onset of the Arctic outbreak) to a widespread 10-15 inches by the 15th-16th (during the heart of the very-coldest readings). Concluding with a brief rundown of how South Central Nebraska finally crawled out from underneath the 10-day crush of ruthless cold, improvement finally got underway on the 17th and trended upward for several days thereafter, with high temperatures at Grand Island/Hastings recovering into the teens on the 17th, 20s on the 18th-19th, 30s on the 20th-21st (ending a 15-day sub-freezing streak), 40s on the 22nd and finally into the 50s on the 23rd (some parts of South Central Nebraska even reached the 60s that day).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The following are the coldest recorded wind chills for the period: on the morning of Feb. 15th: -55 degrees two miles south of Elm Creek; -53 degrees four miles south of Shelton; -46 degrees Kearney Airport AWOS; -43 degrees three miles east of Kearney and 1 mile east of Odessa; -40 degrees six miles east of Kearney; -39 degrees two miles southwest of Shelton; -38 degrees one mile south of Riverdale; -35 degrees at Miller. On the morning of Feb 16th: -54 degrees, 4 miles south of Shelton; -47 degrees, 2 miles south of Elm Creek;-42 degrees, 2 miles southwest of Shelton; -42 degrees, 1 mile east of Odessa; -39 degrees, Kearney Airport AWOS; -37 degrees, Miller; -33 degrees, 6 miles east of Kearney; -30 degrees, 3 miles east-southeast of Odessa.

Factoring in winds (albeit relatively light through the majority of the 10-day period), the most frigid wind chill readings occurred between the evening of the 14th and the morning of the 16th, prompting a long-fuse Wind Chill Warning for all of South Central Nebraska. On both mornings of the 15th and 16th, dozens of automated stations (official and unofficial) recorded wind chill values well down into the -30 to -45 range, and even a few that breached -50. Turning to the large-scale meteorological picture, this prolonged/intense cold outbreak was driven in the mid-upper levels by a parade of troughs circulating around a quasi-stationary parent vortex churning over southern Canada, each one further reinforcing/intensifying the magnitude of Arctic air allowed to spill southward through the central United States. At the surface, persistent, predominantly northerly flow prevailed for days on end as a sprawling Arctic high increasingly-dominated much of the central and northeastern United States. Also contributing to the magnitude of persistent cold in South Central Nebraska was increasingly-deep snow cover, as a series of snow events gradually boosted the average snow depth across the area from generally 2-5 inches on the 5th (just prior to the onset of the Arctic outbreak) to a widespread 10-15 inches by the 15th-16th (during the heart of the very-coldest readings). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very bitter arctic air with ambient temperatures dropping to near zero or below zero and north winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts to near 30 mph on February 14, continued into the morning of February 15.  These factors resulted in extreme wind chill warning criteria reaching -18 degrees or colder for several hours for the northern areas of West Central Texas.  There were a few reports of -20 to -24 degree wind chill readings.  Another period of extreme cold occurred late on February 15 and continued into morning of February 16 mainly across the higher elevation areas of the northern portions of West Central Texas where the winds were a little stronger.  Wind chill temperatures were estimated for some locations since the wind sensors at several weather stations froze because of ice.  There were also widespread power outages during this extreme cold as a result of a failing power grid.   Many residents were left with out power Monday through Tuesday and some even longer.  These very cold temperatures and widespread power outages resulted in several deaths caused by hypothermia.  There was also damage to pipes, public utility systems and water supply systems across the region.  Many were left without water for days.  Dollar damages will be well into the millions across West Central Texas.  The specific and complete information relating to the fatalities and monetary damages will gradually become available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass moved into east-central Colorado and resided in the area for several days. Wind chills warmed during the daytime before dropping to or below Wind Chill Warning criteria during the night. Area overnight wind chills dropped below -25 degrees Fahrenheit with -44 degrees Fahrenheit being the minimum wind chill recorded during this time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overnight variable sustained winds with speeds ranging up to 8 to 14 mph combined with overnight minimum temperatures as cold as -33 degrees Fahrenheit produced wind chills as low as -42 degrees Fahrenheit across Yuma County. The coldest wind chills were observed at the AWOS one mile south-southeast of Yuma, Colorado during the morning of February 15th. Impacts: extreme cold.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air moved into the High Plains following a winter weather system that brought up to 8.5 inches of snow to northeast Colorado over a span of three days. West-southwesterly to northeasterly winds sustained up to 15 mph caused wind chills as low as 25 degrees below zero to occur during the early morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northeasterly winds up to 10 mph combined with cold temperatures as cold as 11 below produced wind chills as low as 25 degrees below zero across Cheyenne County. The coldest wind chills were observed near Aroya, Colorado. Key impacts: cold.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very bitter arctic air with ambient temperatures dropping to near zero or below zero and north winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts to near 30 mph on February 14, continued into the morning of February 15.  These factors resulted in extreme wind chill warning criteria reaching -18 degrees or colder for several hours for the northern areas of West Central Texas.  There were a few reports of -20 to -24 degree wind chill readings.  Another period of extreme cold occurred late on February 15 and continued into morning of February 16 mainly across the higher elevation areas of the northern portions of West Central Texas where the winds were a little stronger.  Wind chill temperatures were estimated for some locations since the wind sensors at several weather stations froze because of ice.  There were also widespread power outages during this extreme cold as a result of a failing power grid.   Many residents were left with out power Monday through Tuesday and some even longer.  These very cold temperatures and widespread power outages resulted in several deaths caused by hypothermia.  There was also damage to pipes, public utility systems and water supply systems across the region.  Many were left without water for days.  Dollar damages will be well into the millions across West Central Texas.  The specific and complete information relating to the fatalities and monetary damages will gradually become available.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind chill temperatures from the Abilene ASOS measured a wind chill temperature of 18 degrees below zero.  The coldest wind chill was -23 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid-February 2021 unleashed a relentless blast of brutal cold, the likes of which South Central Nebraska had not endured in several decades. For the majority of the 24-county area, the 10-day stretch from the 7th-16th marked the overall-coldest 10 days in nearly 38 years...since December 1983 (based on average/mean temperature). In addition to various other official NWS stations (including both automated airport sensors and cooperative observers), this fact rang true for Grand Island and Hastings airports, where the 10-day average temperature from the 7th-16th was -4.7 and -5.5 degrees (F), respectively. Following are various other cold temperature tidbits specifically for Grand Island (126 years of temperature records) and Hastings (114 years of records), although very similar realities applied elsewhere within South Central Nebraska. At Grand Island, the average temperature between the 7th-16th was an incredible 33 degrees below the 30-year normal, as daily highs over the course of the 10 days ranged from -7 to +10, while daily lows ranged from -27 to +1. Furthermore, Grand Island notched nine straight days of sub-zero lows between the 8th-16th (longest such streak since Dec. 1989), and both Grand Island and Hastings spent OVER 60-CONSECUTIVE HOURS BELOW ZERO between the early morning of the 14th and the afternoon/evening of the 16th (had not happened since at least Feb. 1989). At Hastings, the high temperature of -8 on the 15th set a new February record for coldest daily high and was only one-degree short of the record-coldest high (for any month) of -9 set in Dec. 1989. Perhaps most impressively, Hastings plunged to -30 for the low on the 16th, tying its all-time coldest reading first observed way back in Jan. 1912. A few long-time NWS coop observer stations actually set outright all-time coldest low temperatures on the 16th, including York (-34), Superior (-33) and Osceola (-31). Greeley and Ord airport (ASOS) matched the York reading of -34 for the outright-coldest official temperature of this particular cold snap. Factoring in winds (albeit relatively light through the majority of the 10-day period), the most frigid wind chill readings occurred between the evening of the 14th and the morning of the 16th, prompting a long-fuse Wind Chill Warning for all of South Central Nebraska. On both mornings of the 15th and 16th, dozens of automated stations (official and unofficial) recorded wind chill values well down into the -30 to -45 range, and even a few that breached -50. While each morning registered fairly similar and dangerously-cold values area-wide, the morning of the 15th featured both the coldest known official wind chill (-54 at Ord airport ASOS) and unofficial wind chill (-55 from a NDOT sensor two miles south of Elm Creek). ||Focusing on impacts, the local South Central Nebraska area was just a small portion of an expansive swath of the central and southern United States that battled this historic cold, as sub-freezing temperatures surged all the way into south Texas (even promoting a light coating of snow at Galveston). This cold outbreak put a considerable strain on not only the local, but especially the regional power and energy industry. While South Central Nebraska avoided more serious/longer-lasting power disruptions that ravaged many southern states, fairly brief rolling blackouts (typically around 30 minutes) occurred within the area on the 15th-16th, as called for by the Southwest Power Pool (the independent regional transmission organization that manages the electric grid and wholesale power market for portions of 14 central and southern states, including Nebraska). Turning to the large-scale meteorological picture, this prolonged/intense cold outbreak was driven in the mid-upper levels by a parade of troughs circulating around a quasi-stationary parent vortex churning over southern Canada, each one further reinforcing/intensifying the magnitude of Arctic air allowed to spill southward through the central United States. At the surface, persistent, predominantly northerly flow prevailed for days on end as a sprawling Arctic high increasingly-dominated much of the central and northeastern United States. Also contributing to the magnitude of persistent cold in South Central Nebraska was increasingly-deep snow cover, as a series of snow events gradually boosted the average snow depth across the area from generally 2-5 inches on the 5th (just prior to the onset of the Arctic outbreak) to a widespread 10-15 inches by the 15th-16th (during the heart of the very-coldest readings). Concluding with a brief rundown of how South Central Nebraska finally crawled out from underneath the 10-day crush of ruthless cold, improvement finally got underway on the 17th and trended upward for several days thereafter, with high temperatures at Grand Island/Hastings recovering into the teens on the 17th, 20s on the 18th-19th, 30s on the 20th-21st (ending a 15-day sub-freezing streak), 40s on the 22nd and finally into the 50s on the 23rd (some parts of South Central Nebraska even reached the 60s that day).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The following are the coldest recorded wind chills for the period: on the morning of Feb. 15th: -40 degrees five miles west of Ragan; -36 degrees in Alma. On the morning of Feb. 16th: -40 degrees five miles west of Ragan; -33 degrees in Alma.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Snow and sub-zero temperatures blanketed southeastern Wyoming Valentine's Day weekend. Southern mountains and portions out in the high plains measured heavy snowfall coupled then with extreme sub-zero temperatures into the minus teens and twenties for many. Rawlins and Laramie set new daily record low temperatures. With area ranchers in calving season, many had to prepare additional feed and wind breaks to keep herd alive along with snow during portion of the extreme cold.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cow Creek sensor measured wind chill values below minus 30. With area ranchers in calving season, many had to prepare additional feed and wind breaks to keep herd alive along with snow during portion of the extreme cold.
